title: Getting the message across
goals: Use reporting verbs and their patterns accurately (accuse sb of, urge sb to, deny -ing, claim to).
Report conversations, questions and orders with backshifting of tenses, and know when not to apply it.
Attribute information with impersonal structures (is said to, reportedly, allegedly, according to).
Soften claims with hedging (it seems that, arguably, tend to) according to the degree of certainty.
Clarify, summarise and rephrase what others say, and talk about misunderstandings with communication vocabulary.
Write a formal summary of a meeting and an opinion text with a nuanced tone.

learn.title: Reporting verbs and their patterns
learn.html:
At C1 level, say and tell are no longer enough. Reporting verbs encode the intention of the speaker (warn, accuse, admit, insist), and each one requires a different pattern. Learning them as a block (verb + structure) is more effective than learning isolated translations.

PatternTypical verbsExample
verb + that-clauseadmit, claim, insist, point out, maintain, mentionShe pointed out that the deadline had passed.
verb + to + infinitiveclaim, promise, refuse, threaten, offer, agree, demandHe claimed to have met the president.
verb + object + to + infinitiveurge, advise, warn, persuade, encourage, remind, order, inviteThey urged residents to leave the area.
verb + -ingadmit, deny, suggest, recommend, propose, mentionHe denied taking the money.
verb + object + preposition + -ingaccuse sb of, blame sb for, congratulate sb on, criticise sb for, thank sb forShe accused him of leaking the report.
verb + preposition + -ingapologise for, insist on, object to, boast aboutHe insisted on paying.

Important nuances.

  • Deny and admit take -ing (and its perfect form having done when referring to something earlier): She admitted having lied. With claim, by contrast, to + infinitive is used: He claimed to have seen it. The semantic difference also matters: claim distances the speaker from the truth (“he says that…, though I don't believe it”).
  • Suggest and recommend never take object + to. One says suggested (that) I wait (British subjunctive without -s, or with should) or suggested waiting. This is one of the most frequent errors among Spanish speakers, who translate word for word (suggested me to wait is wrong).
  • Warn has two patterns: warn sb to do / not to do (a specific instruction) and warn sb about / against doing (warning of a risk).
  • Verbs such as explain, suggest, announce, describe, mention do not take the recipient directly after the verb: explain the problem to me, not explain me.
  • Insist: insist on doing (about your own action) vs. insist that he (should) leave (about someone else's action); in formal register the subjunctive is used.

watch.wrong: She suggested me to take a break.
watch.right: She suggested (that) I take a break. / She suggested taking a break.
watch.why: Suggest does not take object + to; use a that-clause or -ing.

watch.wrong: They accused him to steal the files.
watch.right: They accused him of stealing the files.

watch.wrong: He apologised me for the delay.
watch.right: He apologised to me for the delay.
watch.why: Apologise to sb for sth: the recipient takes to.
After admit, use -ing (or a that-clause), not an infinitive.

learn.title: Reported speech: backshifting and exceptions
learn.html:
In reported speech the tense usually “moves back” one step from the original words when the reporting verb is in the past. But at advanced level what matters is knowing when not to do it: backshifting is a tool for temporal distance, not a mechanical rule.

OriginalReported (reporting verb in the past)
I work late.She said she worked late.
I am leaving.She said she was leaving.
I have finished.She said she had finished.
I left early.She said she had left / left early.
I will call. / I can help.She said she would call / could help.
You must sign. (obligation)She said I had to sign.
You should / might / could try.No change: She said I should try.

No backshifting is needed if the reporting verb is in the present (She says she works late), if what was said is still true or relevant now (The report stressed that unemployment is rising), or if it is a general fact (He explained that water boils at a lower temperature at altitude). Backshifting in those cases sounds stiff, or even suggests that it is no longer true.

Deictics: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the following day, yesterday → the day before, here → there, this → that, ago → before.

Indirect questions: no inversion and no auxiliary do; if there is no question word, use if / whether: She asked me where I had been. He asked whether I minded. Imperatives: told me to…, asked me not to…

say vs. tell: tell requires a recipient (told me); say does not (said to me, or with no recipient).

watch.wrong: She asked me where was I going.
watch.right: She asked me where I was going.
watch.why: In an indirect question there is no inversion.

watch.wrong: He told that he would be late.
watch.right: He said (that) he would be late. / He told me (that) he would be late.
watch.why: Tell needs a recipient; without one, use say.

watch.wrong: She asked whether did I agree.
watch.why: No auxiliary do in an indirect question.

watch.wrong: He said me that it was urgent.
watch.right: He told me that it was urgent.
watch.why: Say cannot take a personal object directly (said me is wrong); tell can (told me).

learn.title: Impersonal reporting: sources, distance and caution
learn.html:
Very frequent in the press and in formal texts: one reports what “is said” without attributing it to anyone in particular. In Spanish this is handled with phrases equivalent to “it is said that”, “according to” and “apparently”. In English there are several structures, each with a different degree of commitment:

ResourceExampleNuance
It + passive + thatIt is said that the mayor will resign.Formal, impersonal
Subject + passive + to + inf.The mayor is said to be planning to resign.More compact; to have + pp if the event is earlier
according to + sourceAccording to the latest figures, sales fell.Attributes the claim to an external source
reportedlyThe deal was reportedly worth millions.Others say so; the speaker does not verify it
allegedlyThe suspect allegedly forged the signature.Unproven accusation; typical of legal language
apparentlyApparently, the flight was cancelled.“It seems”; slightly more colloquial

Watch out: according to is for other people's sources, never for your own opinion (according to me is a literal translation error; use in my view / as I see it). And allegedly is not a simple, ironic “supposedly”: in English it is a cautious term with legal implications. In Unit 4 we will go deeper into these passives; here what matters is their function as reporting tools.

watch.wrong: According to me, the plan is flawed.
watch.right: In my view, the plan is flawed.
watch.why: According to only introduces other people's sources.

watch.wrong: The minister is said that she resigned.
watch.right: The minister is said to have resigned. / It is said that she resigned.
watch.why: With a personal subject: passive + to have + past participle.

watch.wrong: He is reported to has left the country.
watch.right: He is reported to have left the country.
watch.why: After to comes the base form: have, not has.

watch.wrong: Allegedly, the evidence is totally false, I'm sure.
watch.right: The evidence is, I'm sure, totally false. / Allegedly, the evidence was forged.
watch.why: Allegedly marks something unproven; do not use it to state something with certainty.

learn.title: Hedging: softening with precision
learn.html:
Hedging lets you present a claim with exactly the right degree of certainty. It is not vagueness or weakness: in academic and professional English, stating things without nuance often sounds naïve or aggressive. It is achieved in several layers:

TypeResourcesExample
Appearance verbsseem, appear, tend toPrices tend to rise in winter. He appears to disagree.
Introductory phrasesIt seems/appears that, It would seem that, There appears to beIt would seem that the figures were overstated.
Modalsmay, might, could, would suggestThe data would suggest a link.
Adverbsarguably, presumably, conceivably, broadly, somewhat, relativelyIt is arguably the best film of the decade.
Limitersto some extent, to a certain degree, in some respects, by and largeTo some extent, he is right.
DistancingIt could be argued that, One might say thatIt could be argued that the policy has failed.

Nuances:

  • Arguably means “it can be argued that”; it usually accompanies superlatives and goes before the adjective or at the beginning.
  • Seem and appear + to + infinitive have the same sense as It seems that…; the first is more compact. It would seem is more formal and more cautious than It seems.
  • Do not stack softeners: It would perhaps seem that it could possibly be… sounds evasive. One or two per sentence is enough.
  • Hedging also works as politeness: I tend to think we might want to revisit this is less blunt than This is wrong.

watch.wrong: It seems that he to be right.
watch.right: He seems to be right. / It seems that he is right.
watch.why: Seem + to + infinitive, or it seems + that-clause: do not mix the two.

watch.wrong: Arguably is the best novel of the decade.
watch.right: It is arguably the best novel of the decade.
watch.why: Arguably is an adverb: it needs a subject and a verb in the sentence.

watch.wrong: The results may be suggest a link.
watch.right: The results may suggest a link.
watch.why: After a modal comes the base form, without be.

watch.wrong: To some extent I am agree with you.
watch.right: To some extent I agree with you.
watch.why: Agree is a verb, not an adjective: no be.

learn.title: Summarising, reporting and qualifying
learn.html:
• The gist of it is that… / In a nutshell, … — summarising quickly.
  • If I understood correctly, you're saying that… — checking what you heard before reacting.
  • What she was getting at was… — reporting the intention behind what was said.
  • Let me put it another way: … — rephrasing to clarify.
  • He made it clear that… / She was adamant that… — reporting a firm position.
  • As far as I can tell, … / It would appear that… — presenting your reading with caution.
  • To be fair, … / In fairness, … — qualifying a criticism.
  • Sources close to the company say that… — press formula for unidentified sources.

write.prompt: Write a formal email of 250 to 350 words to your team summarising what was said in a meeting (real or imagined) about a project with problems. Report who said what, using at least six different reporting verbs with their correct patterns, and close with your cautious assessment of the situation. Possible opening: Dear all, Following yesterday's meeting, I would like to summarise…
checklist: At least 6 different reporting verbs (urge, admit, deny, accuse sb of, warn, claim…) with the correct pattern
At least one reported question without inversion
At least 3 hedging resources (it seems that, arguably, tend to, to some extent…)
write.model:
Dear all,

Following yesterday's meeting, I would like to summarise what was said about the delays to the new payment platform.

Priya opened by admitting that the testing phase had taken far longer than anyone had anticipated. Tom then accused the design team of changing the requirements twice without consulting him, an allegation that Laura strongly denied, insisting that every change had been approved in writing. The client's representative warned us that the contract might be cancelled if the platform were not ready by the end of March. She also asked whether we had considered hiring external testers, and Priya replied that she had not budgeted for them.

Several concrete proposals followed. Marcus urged us to freeze the specification immediately, and Laura suggested holding short daily meetings until the launch. Tom apologised for missing the previous deadline and promised to deliver his module by Friday. Finally, our director asked us how soon we could realistically complete the final tests, and nobody offered a firm answer. Some colleagues claimed that two weeks would be enough, although others said they had never worked under such pressure. Everyone agreed that the situation was serious and that communication between the teams would have to improve.

In my own assessment, it seems that the main problem is not technical but organisational. We tend to start tasks before the requirements are clear and, to some extent, the tension between teams has made matters worse. Arguably, the deadline is still achievable, but only if we agree on priorities this week. I would therefore ask everyone to confirm their availability by Wednesday.

Thank you for your cooperation.

Kind regards,

Alex Morgan

write.prompt: Write a 250 to 350-word opinion-style text: «Why do we misunderstand each other at work?». Include an example of a misunderstanding, a reported source using impersonal reporting (is said to, reportedly, according to…), and communication vocabulary (convey, clarify, misconstrue, come across as…).
checklist: 250–350 words with introduction, development and conclusion
At least 2 correct impersonal reporting structures
At least 5 words from v-communication and 2 expressions from v-idioms
According to used only for other people's sources
write.model:
Most of us like to think that we communicate clearly at work. Yet misunderstandings seem to be a daily occurrence and, arguably, they cost organisations far more than most managers realise. Why does it happen so often?

Part of the answer lies in the gap between what we mean and what we convey. Consider a manager who writes, "We should probably revisit this report." She intends a polite suggestion; her employee, however, may well misconstrue it as a gentle order and work all weekend on revisions that nobody wanted. In another version of the story, the employee reads the message as optional and ignores it, and the manager decides he is not committed. Neither of them has done anything unreasonable, but each has got the wrong end of the stick.

Research seems to support this view. Remote teams are said to misinterpret the tone of written messages in as many as half of all cases, and workers are reportedly more likely to assume hostility when an email is brief. According to a survey of several hundred employees, the problem is especially acute across cultures, where one person's directness is another's rudeness. Such findings should, of course, be treated with some caution, but they ring true.

What can be done? To begin with, we tend to underestimate how much context we leave out. Taking a moment to clarify our expectations, and asking colleagues to say back what they have understood, costs little. Equally, we should avoid beating around the bush when a request is important, yet remain aware of how a blunt message may come across as cold. It is not so much a matter of speaking more as of listening better.

In short, workplace misunderstandings are rarely the result of bad intentions. They arise because meaning is not transferred but reconstructed by the listener, and that reconstruction is easy to get wrong.

reading.title: The politeness trap
reading.intro: Read the text about misunderstandings in international teams and answer the questions.
paragraphs: When Marta Lindqvist joined a Mexico City marketing agency as regional director, she assumed that her Scandinavian directness would be an asset. During her first team meeting she told her colleagues that the campaign proposal "does not work" and urged them to start again from scratch. Nobody argued. Afterwards, however, several members of the team admitted feeling hurt, and one of them grumbled to a friend that she had been "publicly dismissed". Marta, who had meant nothing of the sort, was baffled. She had simply conveyed what she considered to be accurate information, in the clearest possible terms. Her intention was to save time, not to offend anyone, and she could not understand why a remark that sounded perfectly neutral in Stockholm had caused such a reaction.

Episodes like this are far from unusual, and they illustrate a point that linguists have been making for decades: communication is rarely about words alone. Every culture has its own conventions for softening bad news, disagreeing with a superior or declining a request. In some workplaces, a sentence such as "That is an interesting idea" is a sincere compliment; in others, it is widely understood to mean that the idea will be quietly buried. English itself is a case in point. British speakers are often said to be among the most indirect communicators in Europe, and a manager who remarks that a report "could perhaps be tightened up a little" is generally understood to be demanding a thorough rewrite. Non-native speakers, who tend to take such phrases at face value, frequently misconstrue them.

Researchers who study international teams argue that the solution is not to abandon one's natural style but to become aware of it. A few practical habits seem to make a considerable difference. Firstly, it helps to paraphrase what you have heard before reacting: "If I understood correctly, you are suggesting that we postpone the launch." This gives the speaker a chance to clarify and prevents small misunderstandings from snowballing. Secondly, hedging is a tool rather than a weakness. Phrases such as "It appears that..." or "Arguably, the main risk is..." allow you to present a view without sounding dogmatic, which is particularly valuable when you are addressing colleagues who may be senior to you. Thirdly, it pays to ask open questions instead of yes-or-no ones, since in many cultures people will say "yes" simply to avoid causing offence.

Marta eventually learned all this the hard way. After a frank conversation with her team, she apologised for having come across as dismissive and promised to give feedback in smaller doses, starting with what was working before turning to what was not. Her colleagues, for their part, agreed to be more explicit about their concerns instead of keeping them to themselves. Six months on, the agency's creative director insists that the team has never worked better together. Marta, meanwhile, claims to have become a more tactful person, though she suspects that her new habits would surprise her friends back in Stockholm. "I haven't lost my directness," she says. "I have simply learned that getting the message across is not the same as saying it."

listening.title: Reading the client's mind
listening.intro: Listen to the conversation between three colleagues. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Right, so, let's go over what the client actually said, because I came away from that call with a very different impression from yours.
Really? I thought it went rather well. Mr. Okafor said he was happy with the prototype and promised to send us feedback by Friday.
Hang on. What he said was that the prototype was interesting. Which, in my experience, is polite for not quite what we had in mind.
Come on, you're reading between the lines a bit too much. He admitted that the design looked a lot better than the previous version.
To be fair, both of you have a point. He did say the design had improved, but he also hinted that the budget might be an issue. He kept referring to the current climate.
That's exactly what I mean. And then he suggested we revisit the timeline, which I took as a warning that they might pull out.
Or it could simply mean he wants a bit more time. Arguably, we're jumping to conclusions.
Maybe. Though he did deny having any problems with us when I asked him point-blank, and people don't usually volunteer that unless something's up.
Fair enough. So what do we do? We can't exactly ring him up and ask whether he's about to cancel.
No, but we can clarify. I'll send a short email summarising what we understood and ask him to confirm. If we've misconstrued anything, he'll tell us.
Good idea. Keep it neutral, though. Something like, we'd like to make sure we've captured your comments correctly.
And I'd put the positive bit up front. If he did like the design, we should say so before we mention the budget.
Agreed. I'll draft it tonight and send it round for you both to look over before it goes out.
Perfect. And let's not beat around the bush in the follow-up call either. I'll ask him straight what the real concern is.
